title: Hacked Code Maps Suno AI’s Music Scraping Pipeline
teaser: Hacked source code reveals Suno AI scraped millions of songs and lyrics from services like YouTube Music, fuelling massive copyright lawsuits.
summary: Leaked source code exposes that AI music generator Suno scraped millions of songs and lyrics from platforms like YouTube Music, Deezer, and Genius, raising severe copyright and legal concerns. The code, allegedly from 2023-2024, suggests a massive data collection effort, noting over 2,013,545 clips from YouTube Music alone. Major record labels allege 'stream ripping' and circumvention of anti-copying measures. Although Suno defends its model training using the 'fair use' doctrine and asserts the code is outdated, the data also reveals a security breach in November 2025, where the hacker accessed customer details. These revelations add substantial detail to ongoing litigation regarding the unauthorized use of copyrighted material.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Hacked Code: Hacked code contains instructions for collecting music and lyrics from several online services in 2023 and 2024. Collection Scale: One leaked file appears to log 2,013,545 clips, while dataset notes assign hundreds of thousands of service hours. Legal Stakes: Record labels allege stream ripping and circumvention, while Suno maintains that the exposed code is outdated. Unresolved Evidence: The files remain unauthenticated, and Suno denies that sensitive customer data was compromised. Hacked code shared with 404 Media shows how AI music generator Suno scraped music and lyrics from online services in 2023 and 2024. Since then Suno and Warner Music Group entered a partnership after Suno's Warner Music settlement in November 2025. Named services include YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius, stock-media marketplace Pond5, and others, while the historical activity predates the major labels' copyright case against Suno . A leaked youtube_music file appears to have logged 2,013,545 ingested clips when last updated. For artists and rights holders, the figure gives a measurable view of the collection attributed to one service. It does not establish how much material entered a production model. Allegations involving millions of songs and lyrics could add factual detail to the copyright fight major labels opened. Suno maintains that the exposed code was outdated and no longer in use, that its models trained on publicly accessible internet files, and that no sensitive personal information was compromised during the November 2025 security incident. The commercial stakes are substantial. Suno raised more than $400 million in June 2026 and reached a $5.4 billion valuation after the financing. Suno completed ists settlement with Warner Music before the files surfaced. How the Alleged Collection Worked Instructions reportedly dated to 2023 and 2024 cover collection from YouTube Music, Deezer, lyrics service Genius, Pond5, Jamendo, Freesound, the International Music Score Library Project, and podcast feeds. Dataset annotations assigned 113,879 hours to YouTube Music, 62,117 hours to Pond5, 17,615 hours to Genius, and 12,287 hours to Deezer. Suno appears to have scraped songs from YouTube using proxy services, which distribute requests through intermediary connections. Searches for a cappella recordings targeted vocal-only audio, while separate instructions pointed to an attempted collection of about one million podcast hours with help from PodcastIndex. Targeted searches, intermediary connections, and service-specific instructions outline a designed acquisition pipeline. Compromised employee credentials may have given the hacker using the alias ellie.191 access to Suno's source code after a November 2025 supply-chain attack. Independent authentication is necessary before courts can treat each instruction or dataset annotation as genuine. Record-label plaintiffs make a more pointed allegation in their litigation: "Suno obtained those copies in the first instance by unlawfully 'stream ripping' them from the popular streaming platform YouTube, and circumventing the technological measures designed specifically to prevent such unauthorized copying." Recording Industry Association of America, representing major record companies (via court filing ) Stream ripping means capturing streamed media as a downloadable file while bypassing copying controls. Courts have not accepted the allegation as fact so far. Authentication could make the claimed method relevant to circumvention, a legal issue separate from whether model training qualifies as fair use. Copyright Stakes and Unresolved Questions Several major labels sued Suno, alleging copyright infringement. Suno later invoked the fair use doctrine argument , arguing that training enables new output rather than substituting for recordings. Specific acquisition mechanics now give courts another disputed issue to assess alongside that defense. Warner Music Group settled its Suno lawsuit and entered a partnership on November 25, 2025 . Licensed model development and opt-in uses under the agreement cover participating artists' names, images, likenesses, voices, and compositions. Future models are planned to compensate participating artists, making consent and payment part of their design. Suno scheduled the first music model developed with industry partners to begin rolling out in the months after June 2026, describing it as a future rollout rather than an available release. Musician Kenneth Blum, better known as Kenny Beats, condemned the alleged collection's impact on working artists: "I can't imagine going into work daily knowing you are stealing from countless struggling musicians. I can't imagine being proud to earn a paycheck obliterating the work and dreams of artists." Kenneth Blum, musician also known as Kenny Beats (via X ) Ellie.191, who shared the details about Suno's scraping, appears to have accessed customer information for hundreds of thousands of users, including contact details and information held by payment processor Stripe. Suno denies that sensitive personal data was compromised.

title: US Marshals arrest the Tate brothers in Miami
teaser: Andrew Tate was arrested in Miami on fresh charges of rape and sex trafficking, including allegations involving 19 charges related to child sexual images.
summary:
Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested in Miami by US Marshals in connection with renewed and serious criminal charges originating from English authorities. Andrew Tate faces an array of accusations, including seven counts of rape, three counts of sex trafficking, and 19 charges concerning sexual images of children. Tristan Tate faces charges including two counts of rape and three of sex trafficking. These new charges build upon 21 existing indictments and investigations across the US and Romania.

Despite being self-proclaimed misogynists and banned from platforms like YouTube, the Tates built online followings by promoting anti-woman sentiments and running controversial online schools. Their activities, which have been investigated since 2015, include teaching men how to 'recruit women into sexual slavery' and running crypto 'pyramid schemes.' The arrests intensify the legal battles surrounding their alleged crimes.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: The manosphere influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested Saturday in Miami by US Marshals in relation to new rape and sex trafficking charges in England. According to the Associated Press , British authorities are seeking the brothers' extradition. The new charges facing Andrew Tate include seven counts of rape, three of sex trafficking, three counts of assault, and "19 charges relating to sexual images of children and extreme 'pornography,'" according to the New York Times . Tristan Tate faces two new charges of rape, one of sexual assault, and three of sex trafficking. This is in addition to the 21 charges already announced in 2025 by British authorities, plus ongoing investigations in Romania and the US. The brothers had previously been indicted in Romania on trafficking and rape charges, but a judge threw the indictment out over procedural issues. Many believe the lifting of travel restrictions on the two and the judges' decision may have been related to a pressure campaign by the Trump administration on the Romanian government. The White House was also accused of intervening on Andrew Tate's behalf last year when customs officials seized his devices. The two are self-proclaimed misogynists who have amassed a following online despite being banned from most platforms for hate speech, including YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram. The two ran an online school that claimed to teach men how to free themselves from " socially induced incarceration " and how to recruit women into "sexual slavery." They've also led an online school on how to make money in crypto, drop shipping, and "scam-adjacent activities," according to Vox , with a pyramid scheme-like structure. The two have repeatedly faced arrest and criminal investigations for their activities dating back to 2015.

title: What to watch for after Jensen Huang’s Japan visit
teaser: Japan is building a 'sovereign AI' factory and commanding its industrial elite to adopt Nvidia's platforms, making the physical world the next frontier for AI.
summary: Nvidia is driving Japan's shift toward 'physical AI' by establishing a comprehensive national infrastructure and forming deep partnerships with Japanese industrial giants. The goal is to revolutionize manufacturing and robotics, allowing machines to perform sophisticated tasks in the real world. Japan's strategic push, backed by a ¥1 trillion commitment, aims for self-reliance in AI and seeks to capture over 30% of the global AI robotics market by 2040. Key projects include Noetra, a sovereign AI platform, and Nvidia's planned 'Vera Rubin AI factory' by 2028. Major Japanese players, including Toyota and Sony, are adopting Nvidia's Cosmos models, accelerating the integration of AI into factory floors and advanced vehicles. This move positions Japan to reclaim its role as a leader in intelligent industry.
author: Kate Park
content: Nvidia's chief Jensen Huang spent two days - July 15 and 16 - in Tokyo, courting Japan's industrial and chip-supply elite, weeks after a keynote in Taiwan, and months after a visit to South Korea . He left with deals spanning Japan's entire tech ecosystem: a national AI factory, partnerships with the country's leading robotics companies, and agreements with the chip-material suppliers powering Nvidia's next generation of AI chips. His message was clear. Nvidia is targeting Japan's factory floor, and many of the country's biggest manufacturers are joining in. AI's next chapter, Huang said, belongs to factory floors, robots, and machines, and he wants Japan to build it. Thirty years ago, a $5 million Sega investment helped keep a near-bankrupt Nvidia afloat; today, Nvidia and Japan's industrial giants need each other again - this time to build the physical-AI era, starting with these three projects: Noetra - Japan's sovereign-AI play. The country doesn't want to run its factories and robots on American or Chinese AI. So, the government pulled together roughly 44 domestic firms, with SoftBank, Sony, NEC and Honda at the core, to build its own AI for robots, vehicles and factory floors. Tokyo is committing up to 1 trillion yen ($6.2 billion) over five years , a bet on homegrown "physical AI", foundation models built to run machines. Japan wants to own the software brain. The hardware to build it, though, still comes from Nvidia. The U.S chip giant is building "a Vera Rubin AI factory", a massive data center packed with its next-generation chips, expected to launch in 2028, with 13,750 Vera CPUs and 27,500 Rubin GPUs , delivering 140 megawatts. Noetra will oversee the effort, with plans to build the data center. Noetra's plan runs in three stages : a reasoning model heavy on Japanese-language skills starting in fiscal 2026; an omni-modal version handling text, images, video, and audio by 2028; and "Real-world Native AI" built to run robots by 2030, released to outside Noetra developers in phases. The robotics coalition - Japan's industrial giants line up behind Cosmos. Nvidia is targeting Japan's factory floor, and many of the country's top robotics and manufacturing players are signing on. Fanuc, Yaskawa, Kawasaki Heavy, Fujitsu, Hitachi, NEC, Sony, SoftBank, Kubota and robotics group AIRoA say they plan to build on Nvidia's Cosmos models, an open-model effort Nvidia started in May with a handful of global AI labs. In Tokyo, Nvidia gave them a reason to commit, unveiling Cosmos 3 Edge , a version of the model that runs on its Jetson Thor chips inside the machines themselves. Some are already testing a shared control system; others, like Honda R&D and Omron, are building on the tools now. "The next frontier of AI is in the physical world, and this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Japan," Huang said in the company's statement. "Japan invented modern manufacturing. Now, it has the opportunity to reinvent it for the age of intelligent industries." Toyota - cars and physical AI. Toyota uses Nvidia chips across much of its stack. It committed its next-generation vehicles to Nvidia's Drive platform at CES in January 2025 ; the newer work extends Nvidia into its manufacturing, where simulations are used to design production lines, into the software that runs its vehicles, and into systems that read road traffic. Toyota's cars will run advanced driver assistance, which steers and brakes but still requires a driver, a more conservative approach than Waymo and Tesla, which are developing systems that rely less on a human driver. Why it matters Huang's visit put physical AI at the center of Japan's industrial strategy, and Tokyo is spending to back it. Facing a shrinking workforce, Japan wants 10 million AI-equipped robots across 18 sectors by 2040, backed by $65 billion in public and private physical-AI investment . The longer game is bigger. Japan's AI Robotics Strategy, released in March, aims to capture more than 30% of the global AI robotics market by 2040, a market Tokyo values at roughly ¥20 trillion, or about $133 billion. METI is funding a domestic foundation model to run the machines, and Noetra's Nvidia-powered factory is where models of that scale, into the trillions of parameters, would be trained. The wager is that Japan's factory-floor data and manufacturing base can do for physical AI Underneath the industrial case is a sovereign one. As the U.S. and China pull ahead in large-scale AI, Tokyo wants its own data, its own compute, and less dependence on infrastructure it doesn't control. Huang appeared on July 16 alongside trade minister Ryosei Akazawa at the government's physical-AI launch, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi joining by video. The Takaichi administration has made AI and semiconductors the centerpiece of a growth plan chasing ¥370 trillion ($2.3 trillion ) in public and private investment by 2040. Noetra's factory - which Nvidia bills as "the world's first national AI infrastructure" - is the clearest bet yet. Japan's push for independence, at least for now, rests on American chips.ndence runs on American silicon. Working the whole room In two days, Huang sat across from nearly every name that matters in Japanese tech - the CEOs of Toyota, Fanuc, Yaskawa, Fujitsu and Kawasaki over lunch, and dozens of supply-chain chiefs over skewers and whisky in a Kanda izakaya. It's the same playbook he ran weeks earlier - a homecoming keynote in Taiwan, fried chicken , and a 50,000-GPU deal in Seoul last fall. This time, it was Tokyo's turn, with the robots, the supply chain, and the chips underneath.

title: The grueling, 630-mile road race where the only fuel is sunlight
teaser: High school students undertake a grueling 630-mile race to prove that solar power can fuel the future, making the Solar Car Challenge a massive STEM showcase.
summary: The annual Solar Car Challenge, celebrating its 30th anniversary, brings together high school students for a grueling, five-day, 630-mile road race in Texas. Students construct solar-powered cars from scratch, learning critical skills ranging from engineering and budgeting to project management. Founded in 1993 by Dr. Lehman Marks, the competition’s primary focus is educational, aiming to build future engineers rather than creating a mass-market product. The challenge recently introduced a 'cruiser' division, pushing students to integrate solar cells into bodies that resemble actual passenger cars. The program has vast reach, having engaged over 85,000 students across 39 states, proving solar technology's viability through academic dedication.
author: Andrew J. Hawkins
content: On July 19th, dozens of teams of high school students will begin a five-day, 630-mile road race from Fort Worth to Fort Stockton in Texas. But this is not your typical contest. The students design and build the cars themselves, using off-the-shelf parts and 3D printed materials. The winner is the team that accumulates the most driven miles. And the only fuel they can use to power their Frankenstein-looking vehicles comes from that mass of incandescent gas that hangs in our sky: the Sun. This year is the 30th anniversary of the annual Solar Car Challenge , a contest that brings together high school students from around the country with the one goal to build the fastest, most efficient solar-powered car. The race was founded in 1993 by Dr. Lehman Marks, a Texas educator with a long-held interest in STEM. Students learn a variety of skills through the challenge, including project management, budgeting, fundraising, and engineering. But mostly, they have to build a race-worthy solar vehicle that can hopefully go the distance. This year is the 30th anniversary of the annual Solar Car Challenge, a contest that brings together high school students from around the country with the one goal to build the solar-powered car that can go the distance Lehman said that the Solar Car Challenge was born out of his frustration with the state of STEM education in the late '80s and early '90s. At the time, he had a group of students who were disengaged and uninspired by learning solely from textbooks, and seeking a way to spark their interest, he accepted an invitation from a friend at the University of North Texas, who was building a collegiate solar car for what was then a brand-new competition. "We went up there and the kids were just mesmerized by the intricacy of the solar project," he told me. "And all the way back from Desmond to Dallas, they kept yelling, 'Doc, won't you please let us build a solar car?'" He relented, but quickly realized that high school students would never be able to compete fairly against college teams because they lacked the technical expertise and financial resources available to universities. Thus, the Solar Car Challenge for high school students was born, with the educational program officially kicking off in 1993 and the first national competition in 1995. 1/6 Some of the vehicles from the 2025 race. Image: Lehman Marks / Solar Car Challenge Since its inception, the program has engaged over 85,000 students across 39 states and multiple countries, including Canada, Mexico, Costa Rica, Spain, and Singapore. There are currently over 260 active high school solar projects. The event alternates formats between on-track and cross-country, with this year's event being a grueling, 630-mile race across Texas. The five-day trek starts July 19th in Fort Worth and travels through the towns of Palestine, Round Rock, Fredericksburg, and San Angelo, before finishing in Fort Stockton. Lehman said that town residents come out and celebrate the teams each time they pass through. "It's not just building a car," Lehman stressed. "It's learning how to officially drive that car. In this coming event, one of the things I've been preaching to the kids is, before you ever get here, you need to put 500 miles in your car. You need to know, will it break? You need to know, even if it breaks, let it break in your own parking lot so you can fix it." The race typically features three categories of competition: classic, advanced, and electric-solar power, in which the teams race electric vehicles that receive energy from stationary solar power stations. This year's challenge introduces a new division: cruiser. In this category, teams build four-seater vehicles with solar arrays integrated directly into the car's body. The decision to create a new division was born out of years of people questioning whether solar cars would ever resemble actual automobiles instead of flat, highly aerodynamic vehicles with a driver often crammed beneath a wide solar panel. Indeed, many of the cars barely resemble anything you would recognize as road-worthy, appearing more like a mix between futuristic spacecraft and high-tech go-karts. "It's not just building a car." - Lehman Marks, Founder of the Solar Car Challenge Lehman said the organizers wanted students to build solar-powered vehicles that looked like real passenger cars, with solar cells integrated into the bodywork itself, room for four passengers, four doors, and a trunk. He believes this helps demonstrate that solar-powered transportation can have practical applications, allowing people to imagine what future solar-assisted passenger vehicles might actually look like. "People would say, 'Oh, this is really neat, but it's not reality,'" he said. "Now we can show them what it could be. And I think that's a step up." Blake Wood is a 17-year-old rising senior from Benbrook Middle-High School in a suburb of Fort Worth. He's also one of the captains of the Old Rip Racing solar car team, one of the few independent teams in the race. Their 14-member team includes students from three different schools, something Wood sees as their biggest strength, because it allows students who otherwise would never have met to collaborate on a shared engineering challenge. Wood says the team began planning approximately a year before the competition. Their earliest work consisted of paper sketches while they studied successful cars from previous years in the Classic Division, which is intended primarily for first- and second-year teams. They analyzed what made those other cars work well and incorporated those ideas into their own initial concepts. As the project progressed, the team improved its computer-aided design (CAD) skills, gradually translating their hand-drawn concepts into digital engineering models. Learning the design software became part of the educational process. "People would say, 'Oh, this is really neat, but it's not reality.'" - Lehman Marks "I think our vehicle, it looks really nice to me," Wood tells me. "It's unfortunate. So we don't really get to see it that often all put together, and it feels like we're always fixing something or making something and then putting something back on, and then we're like, 'Oh no, we need to weld in that area. Let's take that electrical component back off.'" But while battery-electric vehicles have become mainstream, solar cars have remained largely experimental. A number of startups pursuing solar cars have either pivoted to more proven technology or gone bankrupt . Wood says he's optimistic that solar vehicles have real long-term potential, as long as educational competitions like the Solar Car Challenge continue to expose students to renewable energy technologies at an early age. As participants eventually enter professional careers, they can continue developing the innovations needed to make solar transportation commercially viable. 1/4 Vehicles from the 2018 cross-country race. Image: Lehman Marks / Solar Car Challenge "We're making progress," Wood said. "I mean, we have a whole lot of high school students making them, and I think with the right equipment and a little more expertise than maybe all of us have, I think it could definitely be possible." Lehman agrees, pointing to startups like Aptera that are still pursuing the goal of a mass-market solar car. But he said that commercialization has never been the real goal of the Solar Car Challenge. "People say, 'Well, are you trying to build a better solar car?' Between you and me, I'm not," he said. "I'm trying to build a student who is capable, who learns about commitment, dedication to a project, to learn about teamwork, to learn about engineering and battery technology. I'm trying to build a workforce and trying to build engineers." Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: The future of physical games is not looking great
teaser: Industry giants are pouring concrete into the grave of physical games: Sony announced it will stop making physical PS discs starting in 2028.
summary: The video game industry is undergoing a major transition from physical media to digital formats, with key companies accelerating this shift. Sony has announced it will cease manufacturing physical discs for new PlayStation games starting January 2028, a decision met with widespread criticism. Furthermore, Rockstar Games confirmed that the physical edition of Grand Theft Auto VI will use a download code instead of a disc. These moves align with industry trends: Capcom reported 93% digital sales, and Sony noted an 85% digital download ratio for PS4/PS5. Experts and preservationists, like Frank Cifaldi, warn this transition severely impacts consumer rights and the resale market. While major competitors are also shifting (Xbox and Capcom), Nintendo is expected to maintain physical support longer.
author: Jay Peters
content: This is The Stepback , a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on video games and physical media, follow Jay Peters. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers' inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here . As a kid, I relished trips to Best Buy, GameStop, and the nearby mall so that I could browse video games. I loved sifting through games and chatting with my friends at the store about upcoming releases. On the lucky days I actually got a new game from the store, I treasured reading through every page of the manual on the drive home. Over the years, I built up a collection of games that I was proud of. That was a long time ago. Shortly after college, I sold my collection of older games and hardware because I wasn't using them and wanted the money for other things. (Probably weekends out.) Starting with the Nintendo Switch in 2017, I started buying games digitally because it was easier to just download stuff, and I wouldn't have to accumulate physical game cases. Now, I don't own any physical games: My Switch, PlayStation, Xbox, and Steam libraries are all digital. I'm not the only player who has moved to mostly digital games. Digital libraries are increasingly convenient, especially as console makers have made efforts to keep backwards compatibility across generations. Some players can't play physical games at all, as PlayStation and Xbox launched the PS5 and Xbox Series consoles with all-digital console options that were cheaper than the versions with disc drives. On PC, digital libraries through platforms like Steam have been the reality for quite some time. Capcom, one of the biggest publishers around, reported that an astounding 93 percent of its game sales were for digital copies in its last fiscal year - a figure that it expects will rise to 95.4 percent over the fiscal year. Many of the most popular games are only available digitally, like Roblox and Fortnite . For better or worse, video game players overwhelmingly buy and play digital games. But in the span of a week, two industry giants put nails in the coffin of physical games - or perhaps even poured concrete into the grave. On June 24th, Rockstar Games finally put a price tag on Grand Theft Auto VI ahead of its scheduled November 19th release on PS5 and Xbox Series X / S: $79.99 for the base edition and $99.99 for the Ultimate Edition. The prices themselves weren't too unexpected, as even Nintendo has dabbled with $79.99 games for its biggest titles. But what was more shocking was something buried in Rockstar's post : The physical version of the game won't have a disc, instead containing a download code in the box. The announcement was a worrying sign for physical games . Selling games as codes in a box isn't a new concept, but GTA VI will be the biggest game to do it so far. Rockstar's choice could push more publishers to do the same for their future titles. By making the game only available on digital storefronts, players can't easily share it with a friend or sell the game when they're done with it. It's also becoming increasingly clear you can't rely on digital storefronts. Titles can get pulled for things like licensing or the store closing down . This may not be a problem for GTA VI , as Rockstar will almost certainly make sure the game is easily available on many digital platforms for the foreseeable future, especially if it wants to give the game the same kind of legs as the 13-year-old GTA V . But with digital storefronts, you also have to hope that you aren't locked out of your account, even by mistake, and lose access to your games. (In 2023, some PlayStation users were unexpectedly banned through no fault of their own, though Sony eventually restored access to their accounts.) Speaking of PlayStation, just days after Rockstar's news, Sony dropped an even bigger bomb: It announced that, starting January 2028, it would not make physical discs for any new PlayStation games. The decision led to widespread criticism online. Sony and PlayStation got yelled at everywhere online, as Kotaku reported , and the PlayStation account didn't make a new tweet until six days after its announcement about dropping discs. The comments section of Sony's famous 2013 PS4 game sharing ad where one person just hands a disc to another - an ad made after Xbox announced restrictive DRM plans for the Xbox One - is filled with new comments taking jabs at Sony. Heck, Sony itself showed why killing discs is a terrible idea by, on the same day as the disc news, saying that it would be closing the digital stores for the PS3 and the PS Vita . Sony's announcement also drew criticism from retailers and games preservationists . "This is unfortunate news for those who still prefer buying games on physical media, and is certainly a significant hit to consumer rights, the resale market, and game creators whose businesses rely on the physical market," said Frank Cifaldi , executive director of the Video Game History Foundation. Sony's own statement was clear as to why it's making the change. "This is a natural direction for Sony Interactive Entertainment to adapt to consumer trends as the general preference for digital media significantly outpaces physical discs," Sony said in its announcement . "This transition will enable us to align more closely with how most of our community prefers to access and play games today." The company's numbers prove it, too: In the fourth quarter of its 2025 fiscal year, Sony reported that the "Full game software digital download ratio" of games on PS4 and PS5 was 85 percent. We have to see if Grand Theft Auto VI actually releases on November 19th and if it will ever come out on disc. Despite two major delays , it seems likely the game will at least launch as planned, especially because Rockstar gave the game a price and is pushing preorders. We'll also have to see what Microsoft and Nintendo might do. Xbox hasn't announced what it's thinking about for discs for Project Helix, its next generation console, but The Verge 's Tom Warren reports that Xbox will "likely soon" stop making physical discs for Xbox games. However, Warren reports that the company is testing a feature that would let you digitize your physical game collection . Nintendo will probably stick with physical games for a while. According to its last fiscal year report , digital makes up 54.6 percent of game sales, so physical is still a big part of its business. The Switch 2 is also only a year old, and it seems extremely unlikely that Nintendo would stop making physical games for hardware it will be supporting for a long time to come. However, with the Switch 2, Nintendo gives developers the option to sell game-key cards, which are physical carts you can borrow and resell but don't actually have a game's data on them. Instead, they serve as keys to let you download a game to your system. Game stores and preservationists also have to adjust to the fact that physical games are going to be harder to come by. Cifaldi noted that museums and archives have already been preparing for this kind of future "with the expectation that putting discs on a shelf isn't going to be a long-term solution for preserving new games." But he called on trade groups to offer solutions to legally preserve digital content for research - efforts that the Entertainment Software Association has previously opposed . "The industry needs to meaningfully come to the table on this issue, because asking museums to download a copy of Grand Theft Auto VI and hope it'll run in 50 years is not a preservation solution," Cifaldi says. Sony now has to navigate an awkward period where it's launching new games but dealing with pushback from players wanting physical discs. While Sony has been subject to severe blowback after its announcement, it seems unlikely it will reverse course. It's already repurposing its last PlayStation disc-making factory , after all. The PS5 Pro, Sony's top-end PlayStation, does not come with a disc drive; that costs an additional $79. Following a recent price hike that spiked the PS5 Pro's cost to $899.99, that means a PS5 Pro with a disc drive costs nearly $1,000. PlayStation's own studios are now in the awkward spot of having to confirm that physical versions will be on disc, as Insomniac has for September's Marvel's Wolverine and Santa Monica Studio did for God of War Laufey . That Laufey confirmation also signals that the game, which hadn't been given a release window, will launch before January 2028. For music, physical media sales - including CDs - are reportedly on the rise. Comedian Trevor Noah weighed in on PlayStation's news, saying that "for a lot of gamers physical discs are the only way they could afford to play games because they could get them secondhand. You can also give games to your younger siblings, which is a great way to introduce them to the games you were playing." In a post titled "Sony Nerfs Videogame Ownership," the Electronic Frontier Foundation points out that "Unlike other digital media like film and TV, video games require a ton of storage. Access to high speed internet is still abysmal in the US, making the high-speeds needed for digital game downloads a luxury some of us may take for granted." A day after the GTA VI news, Circana analyst Mat Piscatella posted a chart that neatly sums up what's going on: sales of physical games peaked long ago, back in 2009. title: Microsoft Ends SQL Server 2016 Support After 10 Years
teaser: SQL Server 2016 support ended years ago; use ESU until 2029, but migrating to a supported version is critical for security.
summary: SQL Server 2016 reached its end-of-life support on July 14, 2026. Although existing applications can continue running, unsupported deployments no longer receive routine security or product patches, creating a security and compliance risk. To mitigate this, Microsoft offers Extended Security Updates (ESU), a paid program providing high-severity fixes until July 17, 2029. However, ESU is only a temporary bridge and does not restore full support or features. Administrators are strongly advised to plan an immediate migration to modern, supported versions like SQL Server 2022 or 2025.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Support Deadline: SQL Server 2016 support ended on July 14, 2026, while existing installations and application connections continue running. Lost Protection: Unsupported deployments no longer receive regular security updates, product fixes, or standard technical support. Temporary Bridge: Extended Security Updates provide eligible systems with highest-severity patches through July 17, 2029, without restoring full support. Migration Work: Administrators must choose a supported destination and test dependencies, downtime, recovery, performance, and rollback before production cutover. SQL Server 2016 reached end of support on July 14, 2026 , after slightly more than a decade. Existing installations and application connections can continue running, so the deadline does not switch databases off or remotely disable them. Administrators now need to plan the next steps. Remaining deployments no longer receive regular security updates, product fixes, feature improvements, or standard technical support. Administrators must now balance security and compliance risk against the disruption of moving legacy workloads. Unsupported databases may keep working, but newly discovered flaws will not receive routine patches without ESU or a supported migration. Supported paths include SQL Server 2022, generally available since 2022 , SQL Server 2025, Azure SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on Azure virtual machines, or Extended Security Updates as a temporary bridge . What Extended Security Updates Do and Do Not Do Extended Security Updates (ESU), a paid temporary program for highest-severity security fixes, can give eligible deployments up to three years of highest-severity patches . ESU changes the patching window, not SQL Server 2016's support status. It does not add features, restore general troubleshooting, supply unrelated bug fixes, fulfill non-security change requests, or extend the product lifecycle. Servers outside Azure generally connect through Azure Arc , Microsoft's management connection for machines running elsewhere, to subscribe through the Azure portal. Disconnected registration and volume-licensing routes also remain available. SQL Server 2016 entered its fixed lifecycle on June 1, 2016. Mainstream support ended five years before Extended Support expired on July 14, 2026. An earlier SQL Server support transition similarly paired a deadline with a newer database release, but the current timetable still requires its own migration plan. Applications can behave normally after support expires, which can hide the operational change until a vulnerability, compatibility fault, or support request demands an unavailable fix. ESU only buys time for migration rather than being a permanent operating model. SQL Server 2016 has only three temporary patching periods. The official lifecycle table identifies Year 3 as the final ESU period. Microsoft's FAQ sets July 17, 2029 as the outer boundary for highest-severity security updates, so administrators need to complete migration before then.

title: The FBI reportedly won’t investigate ICE anymore
teaser: Amid reports that the FBI will cease investigating ICE confrontations, critics warn that assigning investigations to ICE's own branch guts accountability for rights abuses.
summary: The FBI reportedly plans to stop investigating confrontations involving ICE agents, a change the DHS and DOJ have denied. This shift would likely delegate investigative responsibility to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), an arm of ICE, which the author notes lacks jurisdiction over civil rights violations. This development follows heightened scrutiny regarding violence from ICE, including lethal shootings of civilians in Maine and Texas. While federal agents previously pursued felony assault charges against protesters—many of which fail—the new guidance would effectively leave ICE investigating itself. Critics argue this move significantly reduces accountability, potentially preventing robust investigations into alleged civil rights abuses committed by immigration enforcement agents.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: According to the New York Times , federal agents have been told that the FBI will no longer be investigating confrontations involving ICE agents. The DHS and DOJ denied the change in policy to The Times. The reported change in guidance follows renewed scrutiny of violence by ICE agents who have killed two people in the last two weeks. The shootings in Maine and Texas were just the latest civilian deaths at the hands of ICE agents, who have attempted to intimidate witnesses following its recent spate of high-profile killings. The new guidance would end FBI investigations of assaults against DHS agents. The government has aggressively pursued cases against protesters and others who have had even fleeting and unintentional physical contact with agents. But those felony assault cases routinely fall apart, with nearly half of them ending with an acquittal, the charges being thrown out, or withdrawn, according to a Times analysis . While the FBI investigations are ostensibly to help the government make a case against protesters and others, they often provide evidence against the officers that could be used in future trials against them. Under the change, responsibility for investigating cases involving federal immigration officers would likely fall to Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of ICE, effectively leaving the agency to investigate itself...Homeland Security Investigations does not have jurisdiction to investigate civil rights violations, so putting the change into practice would make it far less likely that shootings of unarmed people by ICE agents would be investigated to determine if the agents broke federal law.

title: Orchid is a delightfully retro and approachable hipster synth
teaser: The Orchid chord organ revives the magic of vintage synth organs, letting songwriters sketch full, rich chords with minimal theory knowledge.
summary: The Telepathic Instruments Orchid is a modern electronic chord organ designed to recapture the simple songwriting magic of vintage instruments like Magnus organs. It allows users to play rich chord progressions effortlessly, making it ideal for aspiring singer-songwriters. Although limited to a one-octave keyboard, its digital nature means it can theoretically play any chord, unlike older models. The Orchid boasts three synth engines (Virtual Analog, FM, and reed piano) and functions as a MIDI controller, but customizing sounds requires purchasing additional software (Pistil, costing $99). While simple to use—with features like key locking and pre-programmed patterns—reviewers note its limitations, including its high price ($649) and lack of true synth design capability, advising that it serves better as a dedicated songwriting tool than a versatile synthesizer.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: In 2017, I bought an old Magnus chord organ off Craigslist for $10. It's one of my favorite music gear purchases. Electric chord organs let you play full chords with just a press of a button, making them perfect for aspiring singer-songwriters or fooling around at home. But chord organs largely fell out of favor in the '80s, as digital keyboards like those from Casio grew in popularity. The Telepathic Instruments Orchid attempts to recapture some of that simple parlor instrument magic. Just like those vintage electric chord organs, the Orchid allows you to play rich chord progressions without having to master a ton of theory or complex fingering. It's not an instrument that demands mastery. It's a way for songwriters to sketch out ideas with minimal fuss, and it expands on the chord organ heritage with distinctly modern twists. $649 The Good Charmingly retro Easy to play Solid variety of sounds Lots of fun The Bad Pricey considering its limitations Only one octave keyboard Customizing sounds requires purchasing additional software The Orchid was designed in collaboration with Kevin Parker of Tame Impala . Aesthetically, it harkens back to '60s brown-and-tan organs by the likes of Magnus and Bontempi . The speaker grill even resembles the fan vents on those classic instruments. It's definitely a spiritual successor, just, you know, a lot more expensive at $649. But where a Magnus organ is limited in how many one-button chords it can play by the number of physical reeds it can hold, the Orchid is all digital and can theoretically play any chord, in any voicing, from any scale. It also means that the Orchid can sound like more than just the beautiful droney cousin of an accordion . Photo: Terrence O'Brien / The Verge For a songwriter, this means you can focus on your lyrics and vocal melody. If, like me, you struggle to sing and play an instrument at the same time, this can take a huge mental load off. The variety of sounds also means that not everything needs to sound like a funeral dirge or a sea shanty, which isn't necessarily the case with an old-school chord organ. If you have even a passing knowledge of music theory (and it would be generous to call mine even passing), you should have little trouble with Orchid. There's a one-octave keyboard and a handful of buttons to the left of it that correspond to different chord types, i.e., major, minor, diminished, major 7th, and so on. Press C and major, and you get a C major. Press F# and 9, and you get an F#9. Simple. The Orchid can really hold your hand if you want it to (and I usually do). You can lock the Orchid to a particular key, so that it will only play chords in the key of E minor or Bb major. That means almost anything you play will at least sound decent and in tune. If your understanding of chord theory is limited, this can really expand your sonic palette with minimal frustration. I often found myself using the chord engine to find a progression I liked as the backbone of a track I could build on top of when jamming in my studio. But the Orchid can do more than just blast out chords in a single block. It has strum, harp, and arpeggiator modes, plus 13 different preprogrammed patterns. My favorite performance mode (as they're called) is "slop," which introduces tiny random timing imperfections that approximate a human actually playing the chord, rather than a machine. The more you turn it up, the more unevenly the notes are struck. Vintage chord organs have a uniquely droney sound, not unlike a particularly buzzy accordion , that, even 40 years later, was still inspiring artists like El-P . But the Orchid can produce a much broader palette of sounds. There are three simple synth engines under the hood: one is a virtual analog (VA) synth, another an FM synth for '80s-style e-pianos and bells, and lastly, a reed piano, perfect for getting those Wurlitzer sounds, but it can also give you more gentle Rhodes electric piano tones as well. I often found myself firing up distorted and heavily reverbed pads on the VA engine and using the Orchid almost like a fidget toy, noodling on simple chord progressions when I needed to focus. You can always connect Orchid to a computer or another synth and use it as a MIDI controller if you want access to its one-key chords but a broader palette of sounds. Photo: Terrence O'Brien / The Verge There are 70 presets (excluding bass patches, which we'll get to in a minute) built into the Orchid, and they cover most of your bases. It's a good thing, too, since there are very few ways to tweak the sounds directly on Orchid. You can change the filter cutoff or tweak the intensity of effects like reverb or phaser, but that's basically it. Instead, if you want to design your own patches, you'll need to spend $99 for the Pistil virtual synth ($50 bundled with the Orchid), which can send custom sounds to Orchid. I've found Pistil to be a bit buggy, and the UI often freezes after transferring patches. Orchid also has a dedicated bass section, separate from the main synth, that you can turn on and off. There are only 12 sounds, but they cover most essentials, from low electric piano octaves to Moog-style synth bass, tuned 808s, and aggressive EDM drones. They can be layered with the main keys to add subtle depth to a chord progression or be played solo. The accompaniment options are where Orchid can become a bit more complicated than just a simple chord machine. If you don't lock it to a specific key, and you set the bass to only play along with chords, then you can have the low-end thump locked to your chord progression, and still add melodic flourishes on top without the bass when you're not pressing any of the chord buttons. Though because of how Orchid handles polyphony - you can't play multiple keys at once - this can be more frustrating than useful, depending on the patch. If a patch has a long decay time, for instance, chords will cut off abruptly if you try to play a solo note. You're better off using the built-in audio looper, which lets you record chord progressions, basslines, and melodies separately, for a bit more flexibility. I am head over heels for the built-in drum machine. It's extremely limited. You can't program a custom beat, you can't tweak the sounds. Yet I think it's basically perfect, even if it would be nice to have the option for user-uploaded beats from within Pistil. It's again inspired by vintage gear from the '70s, namely rhythm machines like the Korg Mini Pops that played preprogrammed beats to accompany home organs. The lo-fi, almost twee sound of these machines is among my favorites in the world of drum machines. The Orchid is fun, sounds good, and is simple to use. But it's also quite limited. You can't design your own sounds without paying extra for the Pistil software. The keyboard is small, and you can't actually play chords on it: You can only play one key at a time, and all the chord voicings come from the chord buttons on the left. That means that if you do know how to play a Dm13 on the piano, for example, you can't do it on the Orchid's keyboard. This is a bit of an annoyance, and one of the key differences between it and a vintage chord organ. It varies from model to model, but my personal Magnus organ only has dedicated buttons for Bb, F, C, A, D, and G major chords. Of course, I can always play any chord I want using the Magnus' regular two-octave keyboard. Photo: Terrence O'Brien / The Verge There are far more capable synths in the $649 price range. But the Orchid isn't trying to compete with the Korg Minilogue or the Arturia MiniFreak . If you want to tinker and design your own synth patches from scratch, spend your money elsewhere. The Orchid isn't for tinkering. It's more of a songwriting tool than a synth. If you're a singer / songwriter looking to escape the cliché of acoustic guitars or upright pianos, the Orchid offers an approachable, if pricey, electronic option. title: From DNA models to mapping the cosmos, AI is changing science
teaser: From mapping DNA to reviewing state law: AI is reshaping scientific discovery and governance across key sectors.
summary: AI is fundamentally transforming scientific research and governance, overcoming traditional hurdles like data overload and resource scarcity. From building massive DNA language models to co-creating AI research assistants used by 15,000 scientists, Stanford HAI faculty are driving this shift. In governance, New York Governor Kathy Hochul is deploying AI to analyze 18 million words of state statutes, flagging outdated requirements. Additionally, Stanford HAI and Stanford d.school are offering immersive programs to help social sector leaders combine human-centered design with AI development.
author: Stanford HAI
content: Governments are spending billions to define their AI independence. HAI Denning Director James Landay explains that the commercial market rushing to meet that demand offers real benefits, but may also provide options that deepen the dependencies it promises to dissolve. As more people turn to chatbots for mental health support, AI developers have come to rely on expert ratings to validate model safety. A new study finds that when psychiatrists rate the same AI responses, their scores diverge in ways that reflect genuinely incompatible clinical frameworks, leaving developers without a reliable method for improving model safety. From helping to build the largest DNA language model ever trained to co-creating an AI research assistant used by 15,000 scientists, Stanford HAI faculty are at the frontier of a fundamental shift in how science gets done. The barriers to scientific discovery have always been the same: too little time, too few resources, too much data to process. AI is changing that. HUMAN-CENTERED PERSPECTIVES New York Governor Kathy Hochul is using AI to comb through 18 million words of state statute, flagging outdated requirements like mandatory fax submissions and telegram notifications. The tools were pioneered by the Stanford RegLab, led by Stanford HAI Associate Director Daniel E. Ho . For PhD students and postdocs charting a path in academic data science, the 2026 Rising Stars Workshop offers a rare opportunity to connect with leading researchers and institutions including Stanford HAI, University of Chicago, Harvard, and UC San Diego. Attend the info session to find out if the program is right for you. Register here → Most AI solutions are designed without a deep understanding of the people they're meant to serve. This fall, Stanford HAI and Stanford d.school are offering social sector leaders a three-day immersive program that combines human-centered design with hands-on AI development. title: I hate that I don’t hate this song made with Suno
teaser: Can AI make great music? 🎵 1010Benja proves generative tech like Suno can shine—but it requires human effort and genius.
summary: Despite being generally critical of AI-generated music, the author praises 1010Benja's track 'Semiramis' Dream,' proving that generative tools like Suno can be used artistically. Benja transparently revealed his process: using his own vocals and elements, feeding them into Suno, and then extensively editing the results in Ableton. He argues that AI is necessary because his creative visions exceed his current financial means. While the author remains skeptical of AI art, Benja's approach demonstrates that by combining human effort with AI technology, the resulting music can be complex and highly compelling, elevating the technology beyond simple 'slop.'
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: I would never go so far as to say there's no place for AI in music (I'm a fan of Holly Herndon, after all). But I generally find music made with generative AI to be offensively boring , especially the outputs of Suno . So I'm having a bit of a tough time processing the fact that I actually quite enjoy 1010Benja's " Semiramis' Dream ." Benja has been unapologetic about his use of generative AI on his latest EP, Time Has Nothing To Do With What You Choose... The other three tracks can't quite hold a candle to what you find on 2024's Ten Total . But the opener "Semiramis' Dream" is infectious. It explodes out of the speakers with a jungle beat and Benja's incredible, obviously human voice front and center. You'd be forgiven for not immediately realizing that the song is the product of Suno. It lacks many of the dead giveaways. Even the most obviously AI part of the song - the choir of backup vocalists - is easily camouflaged amidst the hyperpop-influenced rapid-fire chops. Heavily processed and artificial-sounding vocals are a staple of many modern pop genres and, by leaning into that uncanniness, Benja is able to mask their origins. But Benja isn't hiding. He told Hearing Things in an interview: My friend Patrick Holder did the beat. I recorded the vocals. Then we fed Suno the elements, settled on something, brought it out, edited it on Ableton, and then put it back into Suno. So when you look in Deezer, it marks the song as AI-generated. We're not hiding it. We don't feel any shame about it. Benja's process certainly separates it from the rest of the Suno slop out there. He wrote the lyrics, sang the vocals, and worked with collaborators to perform the music. Then fed that into Suno, took what the AI spit out, brought it into Abelton, edited it, added more layers, fed that back into Suno... rinse repeat ad naseum. Benja estimates he did this a few hundred times for "Semiramis' Dream." While Benja professes to be agnostic about the tools he uses, he is under no illusion that using generative AI doesn't come with ethical baggage. He acknowledges the damage it's doing to the planet, but somewhat nihilistically says we can't stop greedy corporations or put the AI genie back in the bottle: "The good guy doesn't win this one," he says. The only reason I'm using gen at all is because my visions are currently far beyond my means. People have been asking me, "Did you use gen AI for this EP?" I'm like, [sarcastically] "No, I hired a professional children's choir." What are we talking about? I haven't paid rent last month, and I won't pay rent this month. I don't know where the fuck I'm gonna be. It's hard not to empathize with Benja. Despite seeming to be on the verge of a breakout and earning a coveted Best New Music from Pitchfork for Ten Total, he's a struggling artist who has endured periods of homelessness. Still, it's also worth acknowledging that there is little on "Semiramis's Dream" sonically that he couldn't have achieved without AI. Sure, he couldn't hire a children's choir, but it's not like the AI one found throughout the Time Has Nothing To Do With What You Choose... is particularly convincing. A similar effect could be accomplished with some layered performances and smart vocal processing. 1010Benja hasn't converted me - I still remain deeply skeptical of AI art. But he has proven that, in the right hands, Suno doesn't have to be a slop engine.

title: This unpronounceable series of glyphs is an incredible side project from Kieran Hebden (aka Four Tet)
teaser: Four Tet's mysterious 'Wingdings' project features unpronounceable glyphs and incredibly polished soundscapes—a true celebration of modern electronic music.
summary: This deep dive features Kieran Hebden (Four Tet)'s mysterious and unpronounceable project, titled 'Wingdings.' Despite its bizarre glyph-based branding, the music is highly polished and critically acclaimed. Four Tet showcases his signature sound design, blending crushed 8-bit drums, hypnotic handpan grooves, and sharp synth melodies. While suitable for finding your groove (perfect for writing or cleaning), the album avoids being high-octane rave material. Instead, it offers an ecstatic and spiritual celebration, featuring tracks with deep four-on-the-floor beats and metallic gamelan-inspired melodies. 'Wingdings' is widely accessible across major streaming platforms, including Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer, and Qobuz.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: ʅ͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡(̸̢̛̼̞̭͋ͅ)̸͚̰͛̔̾̀̿͒͂:̴͓̞̑̌̂̆̊͋̀:̸͎̟̯̂̓̌　҉　　　　　͡　͞　͞　͞　҉● ࿀ ●  ࿀  ●　　　҉⃝ 　　　⃝͢ ͞　　　͘　͞⃝̕ ͢　　　　̛　⃝ 　　　̸　̡　　͢⃝̧ 　͡　͡　　̀　̧　̢⃝͜ 　 　҉　　͞　͞　⃝͞ 　͞　͡⃝  ⃝҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉ :̶̢͙͙͕̠̩͆(̷̮͍͚̫͚͂̍)̵̳̗̊(　̟̞̝̜̙̘̗̖҉̵̴̨̧̢̡̼̻̺̹̳̲̱̰̯̮̭̬̫̪̩̦̥ What am I supposed to do with this? It's un-Googleable. Unpronounceable. It doesn't even render the same way on various platforms. It looks one way on YouTube Music. Another on Apple Music. And yet another on Bandcamp. Even the artist name ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ is an unpronounceable series of glyphs that would make Prince shake his head. So, from here on out, I'm just going to refer to ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ by his more well-known alias, Four Tet, and the album as Wingdings . My apologies to Kieran Hebden for disregarding his intent, but I've got readers to consider. Also, shoutout to subscriber morgannels for bringing this one to my attention in last week's what are you listening to thread. For years, Hebden has kept this alias somewhat of a secret. But now that this collection of wingdings has racked up millions of listens on services like Spotify, it's get a more formal release with wingdings . Some of the tracks here have been released previously, including track five, which Fred Again dropped during his incredible Boiler Room set as "Feelings," under one of Hebdens' other aliases, KH. Wingdings leans heavily towards Four Tet's dancier outputs. And, despite what the project's origins as some sort of secret b-side dumping ground might lead you to believe, these are not throwaways. They're undeniable, infectious, and highly polished. Four Tet's sense for sound design shines from crushed 8-bit drums to the hypnotic handpan grooves and sharp synth melodies. While the songs are definitely groovy and danceable, they're not high-octane rave-ups, for the most part. Instead, tracks like number seven build to a more ecstatic and spiritual climax as layers pile up and textures demand you turn your eyes towards the sky. Not unlike last week's recommendation, Shall We Go On Sinning So That Grace May Increase? , Wingdings is a celebration. No, I might not drop the triphop-esque track one at the club, but it's perfect for finding your groove while trying to write, or cleaning, or any other activity where you want good vibes and grooves. Track two would feel more at home on a dance floor with its deep four-on-the-floor thump and plucked arpeggios that seem to be constantly climbing off into infinity as house hi-hats tick along. Track three blends metallic gamelan-inspired melodies and ultradeep EDM wubs, while track eight is beautiful comedown ambiance. Four Tet's Wingdings is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music , Spotify , Deezer , and Qobuz . title: The Clapper was a bad smart home gadget — and a viral sensation
teaser: The Clapper: A smart gadget notorious for its failures, yet a massive commercial hit, making its history a lesson in hype vs. reality.
summary: The article recaps the podcast 'Version History' episode dedicated to 'The Clapper,' a smart home device designed to turn gadgets on simply by clapping. Despite technical flaws, including inconsistent functionality and the risk of frying other devices, The Clapper became a significant commercial sensation. The episode explores the device's journey from 'The Great American Turn-On' to its advertising debut. The discussion, featuring Allison Marsh (professor at the University of South Carolina), aims to evaluate whether The Clapper was fundamentally a good product or merely a successful marketing campaign.
author: David Pierce
content: Clap on. Clap off. Well, more like, Clap, pause for half a beat but no longer because otherwise it'll stop hearing you, clap again because you waited too long, clap louder and faster, that didn't work, clap two more times, and suddenly: on. The Clapper didn't always work - and even when it did, it might fry your gadgets in the process - but it managed to become a big hit anyway. On this episode of Version History, we tell the story of The Clapper, from its beginnings as The Great American Turn-On to its debut alongside one of the great advertising campaigns of all time. The Verge 's David Pierce and Victoria Song are joined by Allison Marsh , a writer and professor at The University of South Carolina, to dig into the device's history and legacy, and to try and figure out once and for all whether this was a good product or just a great commercial. This is the sixth and final episode of the fourth season of Version History . If you haven't yet checked out the story of the Harmony remote , the Roomba vacuum , the Nest thermostat , the Keurig coffee maker , or the Philips Hue smart lights, don't miss out! We're taking a few weeks off to get the next batch of episodes ready, so you've got time to catch up. title: Kodak EC35 is a dirt-cheap point-and-shoot film camera
teaser: Kodak releases the EC35, a dirt-cheap $34.99 point-and-shoot camera with a retro flair, capturing a perfect 'disposable' aesthetic.
summary: Reto Project has released the Kodak EC35, an affordable 35mm film point-and-shoot camera priced at $34.99. Despite its low cost, the camera is designed for simple operation, featuring a built-in automatic flash and a sliding lens cover reminiscent of classic Olympus models. Its functional limitations, such as a fixed f/10 aperture and manual winding mechanism, give it a distinctly vintage, 'disposable' aesthetic. The EC35 is available in several fun colors, including butter yellow, lavender, and avocado green.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: Following the success of its $99 Kodak-branded Snapic A1 , Reto Project is releasing the Kodak EC35 , an even more affordable 35mm film camera for just $34.99. The EC35 certainly isn't fancy. Its 25mm acrylic lens with a fixed f/10 aperture and 1/100 shutter speed basically put it on par with a drugstore disposable. The fact that it has a manual wind and rewind only emphasizes that. And you can really lean into that disposable aesthetic thanks to its built-in automatic flash. Unlike the A1, there's no double exposure feature here or zone focusing. The EC35 is designed to require almost no thought to use. Its one special feature is the sliding lens cover, reminiscent of the Olympus Stylus / Mju lineup. It also comes in a bunch of fun colors, including butter yellow, lavender, powder blue, blush pink, and avocado green. The lens covers are a slightly darker shade than the rest of the camera body, giving them some nice subtle contrast. Even the midnight black and vanilla white feature different colored accents, making them slightly more stylish than a disposable camera. Here are a few sample shots from the Kodak EC35:
